S1_incident_reporting.quote: A manufacturer must report any confirmed or reasonably suspected battery-related overheating, fire, thermal runaway, or other thermal safety incident to the competent regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a follow-up investigation report within 30 days. The manufacturer must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident presents a credible safety risk to them or nearby members of the public, and provide immediate instructions where urgent action is needed.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol before market entry and after a material design change. The model must have a failure rate no greater than 5% of tested units. Where results exceed the limit, the regulator may require prompt confirmatory testing and a time-bound corrective-action plan under its oversight before imposing a market restriction, unless an imminent safety risk warrants immediate action.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: New units placed on the market must support secure remote emergency shut-off. Manufacturers must provide a retrofit for installed units that lack this capability, completing the retrofit within six years of this standard taking effect.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: New units placed on the market must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after this standard is adopted.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: When a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units during a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the competent regulator and affected customers, investigate the cause, and submit a corrective-action plan and timeline. The regulator must review the evidence, may require confirmatory testing and interim risk controls, and must require a recall when the evidence indicates a serious safety risk that cannot be adequately mitigated without recall.

document.section_notes: Both red lines are satisfied on both sides: per-model results go to purchasers and the regulator but are not publicly published (NW-1/HC-1), the retrofit deadline is six years (NW-2) and fire suppression starts at 36 months (HC-2). S1 is strong (24 h for all incidents, 72 h customer notice), S2 keeps the 55 °C / 5 % benchmark but softens the consequence to a time-bound regulator-supervised corrective-action plan instead of an immediate ban, and S3/S4 sit in the acceptable middle (72-month retrofit, 36-month suppression). S5 is the weakest section: exceeding 8/100k only triggers notification, investigation and a corrective-action plan, with recall left to the regulator's finding of serious unmitigable risk, so there is no mandatory numeric recall trigger and the corrective path is open-ended.
